platforms.title: Spotting Between Periods: Not Always Serious, Still Worth a Check
platforms.meta_description: Bleeding between periods is usually harmless, but the NHS says always get it checked. Causes, what the GP does, and when to call 111.
platforms.body_html:
You finished your period a week and a half ago, and now there's a smear of blood on your underwear again. It's the kind of thing many people quietly ignore, hoping it sorts itself out. The NHS takes a calm but firm line on it: bleeding from the vagina between periods is not usually serious, but it should always be checked by a doctor. Both halves of that sentence matter. Most causes are easy to treat, yet you can't tell which one you have just by looking at the blood.

It's not just hormones, and it's not usually cancer either

According to the NHS page on vaginal bleeding between periods or after sex, the common causes fall into three groups. The first is hormonal contraception, such as the combined pill. The NHS page on combined pill side effects notes that bleeding between periods, often called breakthrough bleeding, is common in the first few months. The lining of the womb is adjusting to a new, steady hormone level, and small patches of it can shed before your withdrawal bleed is due.

The second group is small growths in and around the womb, such as polyps or fibroids. These are non-cancerous, but they have their own blood supply and can bleed at odd times. The third group is sexually transmitted infections, with chlamydia named first. This one catches people out because, as the NHS chlamydia page puts it, most people who have chlamydia do not have any symptoms. When it does cause symptoms, bleeding after sex or between periods is one of them, so spotting can be the only clue that an infection is there.

Bleeding that happens specifically after sex has a slightly different list. The NHS mentions changes to the surface of the cervix (cervical ectropion), small growths on the cervix, vaginal dryness and, again, STIs. It also says plainly that bleeding between periods or after sex can sometimes be a sign of cancer. That's not a reason to panic. It is the reason the advice is to have any unusual bleeding looked at rather than waiting to see if it stops.

3 things to do before you see the GP

  • Write down when it happens. Note the dates, how heavy it was, and whether it followed sex. A pattern tied to your pill packet points one way; bleeding after sex points another.
  • Check where you are with your contraception. If you started a new pill recently, the NHS says side effects often settle; if they're still a problem after 3 months, a pharmacist or doctor may suggest a different pill, a shorter break, or no break between packs (a tailored regime).
  • Think about STI testing. Because chlamydia is so often silent, a test is worth doing even if you feel fine. If you're under 25, the NHS says you may be able to get a free chlamydia home test kit.

You can see a GP or go straight to a sexual health clinic. The NHS lists what usually happens there: questions about your symptoms and history, a pregnancy test, a blood test, an STI test using a urine sample or a swab, and an examination of the vagina and cervix. If more detail is needed, you may be referred for an ultrasound scan, a colposcopy (a closer look at the cervix) or a hysteroscopy (a camera inside the womb). Treatment then depends on the cause, from switching pills to antibiotics or removing a polyp.

Going back over the warning signs

Most spotting between periods turns out to be the pill settling in, a harmless growth or an infection that clears with treatment. One situation is different. The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if you have recently missed a period, have unusual vaginal bleeding and have pain anywhere in your tummy, including low down in the pelvis. That combination could be an ectopic pregnancy, where a pregnancy grows outside the womb, and it needs checking as soon as possible.

It's also worth separating symptoms from screening. In England, the NHS invites women aged 25 to 64 for cervical screening every 5 years. Screening is designed for people without symptoms, so if you're bleeding between periods or after sex, don't wait for your next invitation letter; book an appointment now. And if your test was recent and normal, that's reassuring but it doesn't replace a check-up for new bleeding.

If the spotting keeps coming back, gets heavier, or you simply feel uneasy about it, that is reason enough to see a GP or sexual health clinic. This article is general health information and does not replace advice from a doctor who knows your history.

Sources: NHS, "Vaginal bleeding between periods or after sex" (reviewed 13 August 2024); NHS, "Combined pill: side effects" (reviewed 15 February 2024); NHS, "Chlamydia" (reviewed 24 October 2024); NHS, "Cervical screening".
